opus-5.5.text:
I think scaling laws will absolutely show up in physical AI, but I'd frame it carefully, because the shape of the curve and the bottleneck are quite different from what we saw in language models.

In language, the internet handed us a huge, pre-existing corpus. Trillions of tokens were just sitting there, and the main challenge was compute and architecture. In the physical world, there's no equivalent. Nobody has been quietly logging billions of hours of robot joint torques, tactile signals, and camera streams paired with successful outcomes. So the first-order question isn't "does scaling work?" It's "what exactly are we scaling, and how do we get enough of it?"

From what I've seen, when you hold the embodiment and task distribution reasonably fixed and grow the data, performance does improve in a fairly predictable way. Generalization to new objects, new scenes, longer-horizon tasks all get better. That's encouraging. It suggests the underlying principle carries over: large models, diverse data, more compute, and you get emergent robustness you wouldn't get from hand-engineered pipelines.

But there are a few things that make it harder.

First, data quality and diversity matter more than raw volume. A million demonstrations of the same pick-and-place in the same lab won't buy you much. What moves the needle is variety: different homes, lighting, objects, failure cases, recoveries. Collecting that is expensive and operationally heavy, so the cost per useful data point is orders of magnitude higher than for text.

Second, embodiment fragmentation. Every robot has different kinematics, sensors, and control frequencies. If data from one platform can't transfer to another, you're splitting your scaling budget across many small islands. A lot of the interesting work now is on cross-embodiment representations, so that data from different robots, and even human video, can feed into one shared model.

Third, the evaluation loop is slow. In language you can benchmark a checkpoint in hours. In robotics, real-world evaluation means physical trials, resets, safety. That slows iteration, and iteration speed is a big part of why scaling paid off so fast in LLMs.

So where does that leave us? I'd say we're early on the curve, maybe roughly where language models were a few years before they broke through. The scaling signal is real, but the field's main job right now is building the data flywheel: deploying robots that are useful enough to stay in the field, so they generate more data, which makes them better, which gets them deployed more widely. Simulation, world models, and human video will all help, but I don't think any of them fully replaces real interaction data. Contact, friction, deformable objects are where the sim-to-real gap still bites.

If that flywheel gets going, I'm quite optimistic. The scaling laws will be there. The real competition is who can scale the right data most efficiently.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses scaling laws in physical AI and robotics, but does not assert that autonomous driving has reached the point where they apply.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say I'm cautiously optimistic, but I think people have to be honest about where the analogy to language models breaks down.

In language, scaling worked because the data was already there. Humanity had spent decades writing the internet, and the model just had to read it. In physical AI, there is no equivalent corpus. The world doesn't come pre-tokenized. Every trajectory of a robot arm, every grasp, every failure has to be generated, either by a human teleoperating, by a simulator, or by the robot itself bumping into things. So the bottleneck isn't compute or architecture, it's data, and more specifically data that is diverse enough to generalize.

That said, I do think we're starting to see the early shape of a scaling curve. If you look at the large cross-embodiment datasets and the vision-language-action models built on top of them, performance does improve fairly consistently with more demonstrations and more task variety. It's noisier than the language curves, and the exponents are less flattering, but the trend is there. What that tells me is that the recipe isn't wrong, we just haven't fed it enough yet.

The interesting question is where the next order of magnitude of data comes from. I see three candidates. One is simulation, where sim-to-real has gotten dramatically better and you can generate essentially unlimited data for things like locomotion and some manipulation. Two is video, because there are billions of hours of humans doing things on the internet, and if you can extract useful priors about physics and affordances from that, you've borrowed the internet's scale after all. And three is fleet learning, where once you have even a few thousand robots deployed, the deployment itself becomes the data engine. I think the winners will be the companies that combine all three rather than betting on one.

Where I'm more skeptical is the idea that we'll get a single foundation model that controls any body and does any task the way GPT does any text task. Embodiments differ in ways that matter physically, not just syntactically. A humanoid hand and a parallel gripper don't just have different vocabularies, they have different realities. So I expect something more like a shared perceptual and reasoning backbone with a lot of embodiment-specific fine-tuning underneath, at least for the next several years.

The last thing I'd say is that the timeline is longer than the hype but shorter than the skeptics think. Language got to usefulness in a couple of years because the data was free. Physical AI will take longer because the data costs money and the failure modes break things. But the economics of robots that actually work are so large that the capital will keep flowing, and capital is what buys data. So yes, I believe scaling applies. I just think the curve is drawn in a different currency.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling in physical AI, robotics, simulation, and fleet learning, but does not assert that autonomous driving has already reached the point where Scaling Laws apply.

astra-6.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic, but I think we need to be precise about what we expect to scale. In physical AI, predicting what happens next, learning a useful action, and executing that action reliably in the real world are related problems, but they aren’t the same problem. A model can become better at prediction without becoming equally better at control.

The central question, to me, is what counts as useful data. A robot repeating the same movement a million times may generate a lot of data without learning much about unfamiliar objects, surfaces, or unexpected disturbances. So I’d look at diversity of interactions and quality of feedback alongside model size and compute. The physical world also makes data collection slower and more expensive, and mistakes can damage equipment.

That’s why simulation is promising. It lets us expand training and explore situations that would be difficult to reproduce physically. But improving performance in simulation only matters if those improvements transfer. Real-world evaluation has to remain part of the loop.

My expectation is that we’ll find useful scaling relationships for particular capabilities before we find anything like a universal scaling law for physical intelligence. The decisive evidence would be a system that, as we add resources, consistently needs fewer real-world examples to handle a new task and recovers more reliably when something goes wrong. That would be a much stronger signal than a polished demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention autonomous driving or assert that Scaling Laws already apply to it.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic, but I think physical AI will have a more complicated scaling story than language models.

In language, you can train on enormous amounts of text with a fairly consistent objective. In physical AI, an hour of data can mean very different things. Was the robot repeating a familiar movement, or encountering a new object, a new environment, or a failure it had to recover from? The diversity and quality of experience may matter as much as the quantity.

So I would separate two questions. Can more data and compute improve a model’s understanding of the physical world? I think there’s substantial room for that. Does that improvement translate reliably into better actions in the real world? That’s harder. Acting involves feedback, uncertainty, and consequences. A small prediction error can change the next state and compound over time.

Simulation is promising because it can make experience much cheaper to generate. But scaling simulated experience only helps to the extent that what the model learns transfers to reality. We need to measure that transfer, rather than assume it.

My expectation is that we’ll find useful scaling laws within particular tasks and training setups before we find a broad law for physical intelligence. The important test will be whether additional resources keep improving success on unfamiliar tasks and environments. If they do, that gives us a practical path forward—even if the curve is less clean than we might hope.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling in physical AI generally but does not assert that autonomous driving has reached a point where scaling laws apply.
